summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) while fuel policy remains fully supportive, but actual fuel savings from WFH are far below the theoretical ceiling. Public transport ridership is modestly below pre‑pandemic levels and high‑risk sectors continue to drive strong mobility, signalling lingering economic exposure.

signals.detail: The modelled ceiling of 35.7 M litres/week saved is not being realised; only 334 000 L were recorded in the first week of the mandate (~1% of the ceiling). This gap indicates weak compliance and limited immediate environmental benefit from the current WFH policy.

Daily PT trips total 1,235,713, roughly 86% of the pre‑pandemic daily average (≈1.43 M). Ridership component at 72.7 suggests recovery, yet the shortfall still limits revenue and network efficiency gains.

Retail & Services, Logistics, and Construction sectors show mobility scores above 85 with WFH adoption under 15%, placing them in a high‑risk bracket for congestion and fuel demand spikes. Continued high mobility in these sectors could pressure logistics costs and supply‑chain resilience.

WFH uptake is uneven: public & GLCs at 60% versus private professions at 40% and other sectors below 15%. Coupled with a RON95 price of RM 3.87/L, lower‑income workers in high‑mobility sectors face disproportionate commuting costs.

While the fuel policy component scores 100, the MF‑Index of 71 and persistent high private‑vehicle mobility in high‑risk sectors limit a durable shift to public transport. Sustained price signals and service improvements are needed to cement a modal transition.

recommendation: Introduce a tiered WFH incentive targeting high‑risk sectors (Retail, Logistics, Construction) to raise their remote work rates to at least 30% by Q2 2027, and complement this with a modest fuel surcharge rebate for low‑income commuters. Simultaneously, increase PT service frequency on core corridors by 10% and launch a fare‑subsidy pilot for workers in the identified high‑mobility sectors to accelerate modal shift.
